title: D-R-Sh

segments.voice: Yesterday, H-L-Ch: halakha, Jewish law, named for walking. Your line was law is a walk. Did you take the one next step? Today, a root for the kind of reading that digs. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

A pregnant woman feels something is wrong. The children inside her are struggling, pushing against each other, and she can't make sense of it. She says, in effect, if this is how it is, why am I? And then she does something. The book of Genesis says: "And she went to inquire of the LORD." That woman is Rebekah, and the verb for what she does is lidrosh, to seek, to ask, to search something out. The same root gives Jewish tradition its word for a searching kind of reading: midrash. Today's root: dalet, resh, shin. D-R-Sh.
screen: `REBEKAH CAN'T MAKE SENSE OF IT.` → `SHE WENT TO INQUIRE.` → `D-R-SH: TO SEEK OUT.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the question. Rebekah doesn't wait for an answer to arrive. She goes looking. Darash is an active verb: you get up, you go, you ask. And she does get an answer, about two nations in her womb. Second, the call. The prophet Amos puts it briefly, dirshuni vichyu: "Seek ye Me, and live." Seeking, there, isn't a hobby. It's how you stay alive. Third, the middle. In Leviticus, Moses is looking into what happened to an offering, and the text doubles the verb: darosh darash, he diligently searched. The Talmud, in tractate Kiddushin, says these two words stand at the midpoint of the Torah's words. Some teachers love that: right at the Torah's center, a man searching. Fourth, the reading. When the rabbis read scripture, they didn't stop at the surface. They asked why a word was spelled oddly, why a story stops where it does, why one verse sits beside another. That seeking is called derash, and the collections of their readings are called midrash. A beit midrash, a house of study, is, by its root, a house of seeking. Midrash can be playful, daring, even surprising. It treats the text as deep enough to keep giving, and the reader as someone who has to go and ask. So this root draws a line from a worried woman to a study hall full of arguments. Both are doing the same thing. They are not willing to leave a hard question alone.
screen: `THE QUESTION: REBEKAH GOES TO ASK.` · `THE CALL: SEEK ME, AND LIVE.` · `THE MIDDLE: DAROSH DARASH.` · `THE READING: A HOUSE OF SEEKING.` · then, large: `מִדְרָשׁ`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: seek one meaning. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a line you know by heart. A verse, a prayer, a lyric, something a parent used to say. Say it to yourself slowly. Then ask it one question, the way the rabbis would. Why this word and not another? Why does it start there? What's missing? Don't rush to an answer. Let the question sit beside the line, and see what rises. If you pray, you can hold Amos's call, seek, and live. The bell holds the time.
D-R-Sh. Dalet, resh, shin: the root of darash, to seek, and of midrash, the rabbis' searching way of reading. Today's word.
Your line: seek. Today, ask one real question you've been leaving alone, out loud, to someone who might know. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Jews study midrash, the rabbis' interpretive readings of scripture, often in a beit midrash, a house of study, and a short teaching on the week's Torah portion is called a d'var Torah or a drash.
